fact: A digital elevation model is a raster layer storing the ground height of each cell, which GIS uses to predict where water will flow and collect.
story:
Juliette's laptop balanced on her knees in the back seat of Ms. Chan's Subaru, the screen tilted away from the window glare. They were two hours out from the city, on a road trip Ms. Chan had organized for the three students who had signed up for the state mapping competition: Juliette, Justin, and Yousif, whose job until now had been choosing the gas station snacks.

The project was Juliette's idea, and it had seemed simple when she proposed it. Overlay the city's flood risk zones on a map of housing values and see who lived where the water would go. Ms. Chan had approved it with one line in the margin of the proposal: "Good question. Answer it honestly." Justin had wanted to map school bus routes instead, and had said so in a tone that made even Yousif wince, though Yousif later texted her: "He's not impugning your idea, he's just mad he didn't have one." She had kept that message, though she wasn't sure why.

The data files had loaded fine at school. Now, in the motel room that first night, something on the map didn't make sense. The flood risk layer showed a band of high risk two miles from the river, in a grid of streets she knew were nowhere near any water. "That has to be a mistake," she said, and both boys came to stand behind her chair, Yousif still holding his toothbrush.

"Maybe the layer's wrong," Justin said. "Maybe somebody drew the polygon in the wrong place."

"Or maybe the water doesn't care where the river is," Yousif said, and grinned, and Juliette told him that wasn't helpful, though she wrote it on the motel notepad anyway, because something about it itched.

She spent the next morning in the motel lobby on the free wifi, going through the layers one at a time. The elevation layer looked different from the others, not shapes and lines but a grid of small squares, each one shaded. When she clicked a single square, a number came up: the height of the ground at that spot. She clicked the square next to it. A lower number. She clicked her way downhill, square by square, out of curiosity more than strategy, and the squares led her away from the river, north, down a long shallow slope, until they pooled in exactly the grid of streets shaded red on the flood layer.

"Look at this," she said when the boys came down for the continental breakfast. She turned the laptop toward them. "This layer, the grid one. It's called a digital elevation model."

"Sounds like something a polymath would invent," Yousif said, stealing her muffin.

"Each little square stores the ground height for that spot," she said, dragging the cursor across the slope. "So the software can figure out where water will flow and collect. It goes downhill. All those streets are lower than everything around them, even though they're far from the river, so that's where the water ends up."

Justin leaned in, muffin forgotten. "So the flood map isn't wrong."

"The flood map is the honest one." She zoomed out, and the housing layer came back on under everything, and the cheap blocks and the red blocks sat on top of each other like they had been cut from the same paper.

That afternoon Ms. Chan drove them into the city itself to look at the streets. She parked at the edge of the neighborhood and let them walk. The houses were small and close together, some with water stains on the lower courses of brick, and Juliette found herself checking the height of every porch step against every other one, doing the elevation model in her head, square by square. An old man watering a garden asked what they were looking at, and Yousif said, "School project," and the man said, "Flood study? Third one this year. Nobody's fixed anything yet," and went back inside.

At the competition the next day their presentation went fourth. Juliette had built the maps herself, but she let Justin do half the talking, and he did it well, and afterward he said, without quite looking at her, "Your idea was better than the bus routes," which was as close as he got to anything. The judges asked one question she couldn't fully answer: whether the elevation data was recent enough to trust after all the new construction. She said she didn't know, that the layer was five years old and the houses were older than that, but that she wouldn't claim more certainty than the data had.

They didn't win. The team that won had mapped trail erosion with drone photos, and their posters were glossy, and during the feedback session one judge had been almost vitriolic about how "policy-flavored" projects exceeded the scope of the contest, which Ms. Chan later called nonsense in the parking lot, though she said it quietly, unlocking the car.

On the drive home, with the boys asleep against the windows, Juliette opened her phone and found she had drafted a message to Ms. Chan hours ago, in the convention center bathroom, and never sent it. It said: "I keep thinking about the old man who said nobody's fixed anything. I wanted the map to feel like proof, but a map isn't a fix, it's an argument, and I don't know who I'm arguing with yet. Maybe that's enough for now and maybe it isn't." She read it twice, then sent it, then put the phone face down on her knee.

Ms. Chan's reply came while they were still an hour from home, and Juliette read it in the blue dashboard light: "Check your elevation layer. Then ask yourself who lives in the low squares and who drew the zoning. See you Monday." Juliette looked out at the dark fields going by, opened the laptop on her knees, and began, carefully, to add a new layer.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Plain-language guidance recommends the active voice, in which the subject does the action, as in 'I missed the deadline', because it makes clear who did what.
story:
The bakery smelled of scorched sugar and dish soap, and the woman behind the counter, whose name tag read "Manager" and nothing else, slid a sheet of paper across the glass case. "Most applicants I just talk to," she said. "You applied for the customer service shift, so here's the real test. A customer's birthday cake came out with the wrong name on it. Write her an email. Fifteen minutes. I'll be in the back."

Zoe sat at the wobbly table by the window and read the scenario twice. The customer, Mrs. Okafor, had ordered a cake for her daughter's party, picked it up, and only discovered at home that it said "Amara" instead of "Amina." She had called, upset, and hung up before anyone finished apologizing. Zoe's job was to fix it in writing.

She began drafting in her head, and the first sentence that arrived was a beautiful one: Mistakes were made in the processing of your order. It sounded professional. It sounded like the letters that came from the school board when the buses failed, that elegant fog that rolled over everything. She had almost typed it when she remembered Kristen, in the library in June, reading aloud from a plain-language handout Mr. Côté had photocopied for their civics essays. "Use the active voice," Kristen had recited, chewing her pen. "The subject does the action. Like 'I missed the deadline.'" Zoe had rolled her eyes at the time and asked if he'd also be grading their souls. Melodie had laughed so hard the librarian came over.

But now she sat with the sentence on the screen, and the sentence sat there doing nothing, admitting nothing, belonging to no one. Whoever had made the mistake, and Zoe was fairly sure it would be whoever held this job, was hiding inside it. Mrs. Okafor would read it and know, correctly, that she was being managed.

So Zoe deleted it. She wrote: I misspelled your daughter's name on the cake. Then she stopped, because she hadn't actually made that cake. She had never worked here. She could not honestly claim an error she hadn't committed, and she could not honestly deny that the bakery had made it. She looked at the door to the back room, at the flour dust in the light, and decided she could be specific without lying: We misspelled your daughter's name on the cake. It was our error, and I am sorry it reached your daughter's party. The "we" was true whoever she turned out to be, and the "I" took the apology personally, which was the part that mattered.

The rest came faster, though not easily. She wanted to offer a replacement cake, but she didn't know if she'd have the authority, so she offered what she could safely offer and framed the rest as a question: "May we bake a new cake for your family, at no charge, on any date you choose?" Then, because Melodie's mother worked in insurance and once said over dinner that a good apology says what will change, Zoe added a line about how the order form would be read back to customers at pickup from now on. It was a promise she might not be able to keep. She wrote it anyway, then softened it to "I would like to propose," which was maybe cowardly, and then left it, out of time to be brave twice in one email.

The manager came out wiping her hands on a towel. "Done? Read me the first line."

"We misspelled your daughter's name on the cake. It was our error, and I am sorry it reached your daughter's party."

The manager stopped wiping. "Huh. Most people write 'mistakes were made.'"

Zoe's face went hot, as if she'd been caught at something. "I almost did," she said. "But then it doesn't say who did what. You can't tell who's apologizing." She hesitated, because the next part she couldn't prove. "I think that's why the plain-language people say to use the active voice. The subject does the action. Like 'I missed the deadline.'" She heard Kristen's voice in it, slightly, and hoped the manager wouldn't ask where she'd learned it, because "civics class" sounded like an anachronistic answer to a bakery, like citing Blackstone over a croissant.

The manager read the rest of the email in silence, and Zoe watched her face for a verdict and got nothing readable, which was its own kind of education. The fifteen minutes had contained a whole morass of choices she hadn't anticipated: the passive voice had offered her cover, and she had given it up, and she still didn't know if giving up cover was wisdom or just a smaller salary for the same work.

"Can you start Saturday?" the manager said. "Nine o'clock. And bring that voice with you, because I am not writing the apology emails in this shop anymore."

Zoe said, "Saturday, nine," and picked up her pen to write it down, though she knew she would remember it anyway.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed.
story:
The fluorescent hum of the pharmacy made everything look already decided, and Madison stood in aisle three with a basket she had not yet put anything into. Ms. Wijaya had agreed to let her shadow the counter on Thursday afternoons, part of the peer health elective that Madison had signed up for mostly because Farrah had dared her to, and that she had kept attending for reasons she could not yet articulate. Her job was simple in the way that simple things are not: learn the facts well enough to explain them to someone her own age, without a lecture, without flinching.

The first weeks had been vocabulary. Contraception was not one thing but a family of things, each with its own arithmetic, and Ms. Wijaya insisted that Madison learn the arithmetic rather than the slogans. In the back room there was a laminated chart, and Madison had copied the relevant line into her notebook in her smallest handwriting, the way she wrote things she was afraid of forgetting.

She was restocking the shelf of cold remedies when Selina came in. It was nearly closing. Selina moved through the store like someone trying not to be seen by the cameras, or by herself, and she did not look at the baskets. Madison watched her stop at the far end of aisle five, where the tests were, watched her stand there long enough that a person could have read the whole chart twice.

"You're here late," Madison said, coming up beside her, and Selina startled so hard the shelf rattled.

"Don't do that." Selina's laugh came out wrong, an acerbic little bark with nothing behind it. Then, quieter, "Is Ms. Wijaya here?"

"She's in the back. Why?"

Selina's face did the thing faces do when they are deciding how much truth they can afford. She was on the pill, she said. Had been for months. That part was fine, that part she had handled, except that her period was four days late and she could not stop doing the math in her head, and the math kept coming out different every time.

"Have you missed any doses?" Madison asked. She kept her voice level because that was the training, and also because she was suddenly aware that this was the test, not the elective, this.

"Like, one. Maybe two, over the whole pack. When we had finals. I doubled up the next day, like the leaflet says."

Madison did not answer right away. In the silence she could hear the refrigerator with the vaccines cycling on, could hear a car passing outside. She took out her notebook, which felt absurd, and opened it to the page anyway.

"I wrote this down in October," she said. "With typical use, about seven in a hundred people relying on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, and it's often because doses get missed." She let Selina read it herself. "That's the real number. Not the perfect-use one on the poster. Typical use means people like us, with finals."

Selina stared at the page. "So seven in a hundred means I'm fine?"

"It means I can't tell you that. Nobody can tell you that from here." Madison's whole training was about not pretending certainty she did not have, and her teacher had even given the habit a name, epistemology, the study of how you know what you know, and Madison had thought the word was ridiculous until this moment, when knowing the limits of what she knew was the only honest thing she could offer. "It means the odds are on your side and the way to find out is a test, and if you want, there's a clinic on Corbett Street that does infections and everything else, no referral, you can just book."

"Would you come with me? After?" Selina's voice had dropped to almost nothing, and her whole face was a kind of beseeching Madison had never seen from her before, not in eleven years of shared classrooms and borrowed lunches. "Not for the test. Just to book it. I'll say the words better if you're there."

Madison looked down the aisle toward the counter, where the light was already half off above register two. Ms. Wijaya appeared at the end of the row, reading glasses pushed up into her hair, saying nothing, waiting with the particular patience of someone who has watched a hundred girls stand where Selina was standing.

"Take your time choosing," Madison said. "I'll be at the counter when you're ready."

She walked over and set her notebook down in front of Ms. Wijaya, open to the page with the number on it, and Ms. Wijaya looked at it, then at her, and pulled a stool around so there would be two seats behind the counter instead of one.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts.
story:
The gym smelled of rubber and cold coffee, and the twelve eleven-year-olds on the court could not complete a chest pass without bouncing it off someone's shin. Mia stood at the sideline with her clipboard, watching her carefully typed drill fall apart for the third Saturday in a row. She had diagrammed everything: the passing lanes, the pivot foot, the follow-through. The drills were clean on paper and useless in practice, and Laura kept glancing over from the far basket as if to ask whether Mia was going to admit it.

"Stop," Mia called, and the kids stalled mid-scramble, grateful for the pause. "When you pass, bend your wrists back more. Cock them, then snap them forward." She demonstrated, exaggerating the hinge of her own hand. Twelve faces nodded. Twelve bodies went back to throwing the ball at knees and shoulders. By the end of the hour, the passes were, if anything, worse, stiffer, the kids so busy monitoring their own wrists that they forgot their teammates existed.

Afterward, while she stacked cones in the equipment cage, she kept turning the failure over. She had assumed the problem was mechanical, that naming the body part would fix the body part. But the correlation between her instructions and their improvement had run exactly backwards. She thought about her chemistry teacher, Mr. Petrov, who coached the boys' team on Tuesdays and who had once told her, when she'd asked him about lesson planning, "You have to historicize your own assumptions. Ask where they came from before you trust them." Hers, she realized, had come from one afternoon years ago.

It had been the winter she was eleven, the same age as these kids, standing on this same court with the ball sweating in her hands. Her coach had shouted corrections at her all practice: elbow in, fingers spread, knees bent. She had gone home and cried into her sleeve, and she had quit thinking of herself as a passer entirely. What had actually rescued her was a pickup game in the spring, when a boy named Taha had said, only once, "Just hit my hands. Don't look at the ball, look at my hands." She had thrown him a pass so clean it had surprised them both. She had never connected that moment to the miserable winter before it, not until now, stacking cones in the dark.

On Monday she found Mr. Petrov in the chemistry prep room and asked, carefully, whether he'd ever heard of a researcher named Gabriele Wulf. He raised an eyebrow. "The focus-of-attention work," he said. "I've read some. Why?" She told him about the wrists. He almost smiled. "So you gave them an internal focus. What does Wulf say learners do better with?" She had the article folded in her back pocket, printed from the library database, its margins already soft from handling. "An external one," she said. "The research found that learners usually improve faster when they're told to focus on the effect of the movement, on the target, rather than on their own body parts." Saying it out loud felt like handing over the answer to a test she had already failed once.

Saturday came, and Mia stood in front of the twelve kids with a strip of masking tape on each of their palms. "Forget your wrists," she said. "Forget your arms. When you pass, hit your teammate's hands. That's all. The ball goes to the tape, not to the person." Laura, rebounding on the sideline, gave her a look that meant she thought this was too simple to work. The first five minutes were ragged. Then a small girl named nothing anyone used, just K, fired a pass that slapped square into a boy's taped palms, and the sound of it carried across the gym like a door closing properly for once.

By the end of the hour, the passing drill ran without Mia saying a word. She stood at half court with her dead clipboard and tried to be honest with herself about what she didn't know. Maybe it was the tape. Maybe it was novelty, or the kids finally sleeping enough, or a dozen causes she couldn't separate, and she was wary of inventing causality just because the result had come out right. Wulf's finding held for the learners she'd studied; whether it would hold for these twelve, next week, when the tape lost its novelty, was a question she could only answer by watching.

"Same time next week?" Laura asked, hauling the ball bag toward the cage.

Mia peeled a strip of tape off her own palm, folded it once, and put it in her pocket with the margins-soft article. "Bring two rolls," she said. "I'm taping the wall, too. They need to hear it hit a spot."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java fields left uninitialized get default values: 0 for numbers, false for booleans, and null for object references.
story:
The computer lab smelled like warm dust and dry-erase marker, and Carter had forty minutes to make a class work that did not yet exist. Ms. Wright had written the assignment on the board in her square, patient handwriting: a Student class in Java, fields private, getters public, a constructor, and a test. She had a way of standing beside the board with the marker capped in her fist, as though the whole project of object-oriented programming were a favour she was doing the room.

Carter typed the fields first, the way he always did, because fields felt like the bones of a thing. Private String name. Private int age. Private boolean enrolled. Then the getters, then the constructor, and it was here that he stopped, because Manraj leaned over from the next machine and said, "Your constructor's empty."

"It compiles," Carter said, which was his usual defense, and Manraj laughed the particular laugh of someone who has watched a bridge get built with no bolts.

"It compiles," Manraj agreed, "the way an empty envelope mails."

Mathew, two rows back, said nothing. Mathew had finished early, which was itself unremarkable, but he had then turned his monitor fifteen degrees away from the room, which was not. He kept glancing at the door as if expecting a fire drill. Carter filed it under things to worry about later, because Ms. Wright was walking the rows now, and she had a rule about asking questions only when you had earned them, which was a cerebral way of saying she wanted you stuck first.

Carter wrote the test. He made a Student, called getName, and printed it. The output window blinked, ran, and produced a single word: null. He sat with that for a moment. He had expected an error, some red text telling him he'd forgotten something, but Java had simply handed him a value, calm as a cashier giving change. He tried getAge and got 0. He tried isEnrolled and got false. Three fields, three strange quiet answers, and it dawned on him slowly that the language had not failed him. It had decided. Somewhere in the design of it, someone had chosen what an unset thing should be, and the choice was these defaults, and his empty constructor had let them all through.

"Your name prints null," he said to Manraj, almost admiring.

"Mine prints Manraj," Manraj said. "Because I set it."

"Everything I didn't set still has a value," Carter said. "That's the part that gets me. It's not nothing. It's a specific nothing." He was thinking of his father, who called programming a sinecure for people who liked being paid to sit still, and how wrong that felt now, sitting still with three wrong numbers and a pulse.

Then the withheld thing surfaced. Ms. Wright stopped at Mathew's terminal and asked to see his test file, and Mathew turned the monitor back with the reluctance of a man revealing a magic trick gone wrong. On his screen was a test, elaborate and confident, that called methods on a Student object and printed expected values, and every one of them assumed the fields had been set. The test failed everywhere, and it failed for the same reason Carter's had printed null, except Mathew hadn't known that reason existed. He had assumed unset fields were empty, dangerous, unpredictable. They were worse. They were reliable.

"I wrote a whole grading harness," Mathew said, wounded. "I was going to test everyone's class."

"Everyone's," Ms. Wright repeated, and let the word sit there, and the room got very interested in its own keyboards. Because a harness meant Mathew had planned to run his test against his classmates' files, and somewhere in his directory, Carter realized, sat a copy of Carter's class from the shared folder, the one with the empty constructor, the one that would feed his harness a stream of nulls and zeros and falses, a whole student body of ghosts that had names Mathew believed in.

Ms. Wright said, "Show me what it prints," and Mathew ran it, and the output unspooled, name after name, each one null. The screen filled with them. Manraj said, "You built a roster of nobody," and Mathew put his head down on his folded arms, and even Ms. Wright's mouth did something it was trying not to do.

Carter looked at his own screen, at his three quiet defaults, and understood he had learned the fact twice, once as a bug and once as a design, and could not yet say which it really was. He began filling in his constructor. Outside the lab door, footsteps went past without stopping, and Mathew said, muffled, "Can I borrow your getters?"

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) held that a public official suing for libel must prove actual malice: that the statement was known to be false or made with reckless disregard for truth.
story:
The town hall meeting had been scheduled for seven, but by six forty the folding chairs were full and people stood along the walls, and Kate sat in the back row with her briefcase open on her knees, mouthing the first line of her argument. In two weeks she would stand before a panel of lawyers acting as justices and argue a mock case about a newspaper that had printed something false about a mayor, and Ms. Campbell had told her, flatly, that whoever argued both sides best would earn the seat at the regional competition. Kate had wanted that seat since September, when she had watched a senior take it and walk off with a scholarship mention in the local paper. Now she flipped her notecards and waited for the meeting to start, because the agenda item before hers was the proposal to sequester the student council's discretionary fund, and her debate partner Kolby had insisted she sit through it to learn how adults argued badly.

They argued badly. A man in a windbreaker accused the treasurer of hiding money; the treasurer said the man hadn't read the budget; someone's grandmother stood up and asked what discretionary even meant, and nobody answered her. Kate took notes anyway. She wrote that people trusted a tone more than a fact, that the room turned toward whoever sounded certain, and then she underlined it twice, because she suspected this was what her case was actually about.

Kolby leaned over her notebook. "You're not even listening."

"I'm listening to how it works. Watch. That guy's going to say something he can't prove, and half the room will believe him anyway."

"That's my point," Kolby said. "That's the whole point of your case."

The case was this: a fictional paper had reported that a mayor embezzled funds, then printed a correction that got the number wrong, and the mayor sued. Kate had drawn the side arguing that the paper should not be punished. Her problem was that she kept losing to Sebastian in practice, because Sebastian argued the mayor's side with a kind of clean outrage, and outrage was easy, and Kate's side required her to defend a newspaper that had been wrong. She had spent a week trying to find the law that made being wrong survivable.

She found it on a Thursday, alone in the library, in a case she had skipped past twice. New York Times v. Sullivan, 1964. She read the holding three times, copying it onto a card, and when she got to the phrase actual malice she stopped, because it did not mean what she would have guessed. A public official suing for libel had to prove the statement was known to be false or made with reckless disregard for truth. She said it out loud in the empty periodicals room, just to hear whether it held together, and it did, and she felt the specific pleasure of a door coming unlocked. The paper's honest error was not malice. Her whole side of the case stood on that distinction. She texted Kolby one word: found it.

The shift came at the next practice, which is where Kolby's part of this begins, because Kolby had decided to watch Kate argue rather than listen to her, and the difference mattered. Kolby had read the same case two days after Kate found it, out of loyalty or rivalry, and had noticed something Kate hadn't yet said aloud: the rule protected public officials, and the mock case's mayor was one, but the rule's logic crept outward toward everyone, toward the grandmother at the town hall, toward people with no power to answer a headline. Kolby wasn't sure that was fair. Kolby was also not sure it was unfair.

In the classroom after last period, Kate stood at the front and delivered her rebuttal to Sebastian's outrage. "The paper was wrong about the amount," she said. "Being wrong isn't enough. Under New York Times versus Sullivan, the mayor has to prove actual malice. That means the statement was known to be false or made with reckless disregard for truth. He can't prove that, because the reporter called three sources before printing." Sebastian shifted. Ms. Campbell, grading at her desk, did not look up, but her pen stopped.

"Okay," Sebastian said slowly, "so a paper can smear me and say sorry."

"Not if you're a public official and they knew it was false. Then they pay."

"And if I'm not an official?"

Kate opened her mouth and closed it. Kolby, watching from the second row, saw the exact moment the win stopped feeling like a win, saw Kate glance down at her cards and then past them at the window, the way she did when a problem followed her out of the room. Kolby almost said it then, the thing about the rule spreading past the people it was written for, a pernicious generosity, maybe, or maybe just the price of a free press, but the bell rang and Sebastian was already packing his bag and saying he'd find a law for his side too, something old, some primogeniture of reputation, inherited harm, he'd figure it out.

Kate walked out beside Kolby, cards squared in her hand, and at the door Kolby said, "You're going to get the seat."

"You don't know that."

"You're the only one who can argue both sides."

Kate stopped on the steps. The parking lot was loud with buses, and she was already rewriting her closing in her head, already planning to concede, out loud, to the justices, that the rule protected the careless as well as the honest, and to say she still believed it was better than the alternative, though she could not yet prove the better part. "Ask me after regionals," she said, and started down toward the bus.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the traditional colour wheel, like red and green, and placed side by side they make each other look brighter.
story:
Justin spread the printout of Kahlo's Self-Portrait on the Borderline between Mexico and the United States across the kitchen table and weighed the corners down with his mother's casserole dish, because the paper kept curling like it wanted to escape the assignment too. Ms. Goldberg wanted a formal analysis by Monday: colour, composition, symbolism, no biography, no "I feel." He had a highlighter, a legal pad, and the growing suspicion that he had nothing to say.

Lane had invited himself over under the pretence of studying, but he'd been lying on the living room couch for an hour now, tossing a tennis ball at the ceiling and catching it, occasionally missing. "You know what I want," Lane called. "The midnight screening. Anaelle's already in, you're the holdout. This is a once in a generation cultural event, Justin."

"You said that about the last one." Justin leaned over the painting. The left half was green, jungle, roots, a fertility idol. The right half was grey machinery, smoke, the stars and stripes bleached into a fog. And in the middle stood Kahlo in a pink dress, holding a cigarette in one hand and a Mexican flag in the other, rooted on a plinth like a museum artifact of herself. Why was she standing on a pedestal in her own painting? He wrote the question down and underlined it, then felt embarrassed and stopped underlining.

The ball bounced off the ceiling. "The essay's four hundred words," Lane said, appearing in the kitchen doorway to raid the fridge. "You could write four hundred words in your sleep. You've written more than that arguing with me about the Lakers." He drank orange juice straight from the carton, which Justin's mother had banned him from doing the previous Tuesday.

"It's not the words, it's the seeing." Justin tapped the reproduction. "Look here. These red flowers against all this green. When I stare at them they sort of, I don't know, they hum. Is that a thing, or did I stare too long?" Lane shrugged and, because he was constitutionally incapable of standing still while a phone existed in his pocket, looked it up. He read aloud in his flat mocking-voice: "Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the colour wheel, like red and green, and placed side by side they make each other look brighter." He lowered the phone. "So it's a thing. Congrats, your eyes work."

Justin took the phone and read it twice himself, because Lane's voice was not a reliable medium for information. So the red and the green weren't just decorative; they were positioned, deliberate, a choice made in the opposite direction from the grey half, where nothing brightened anything. He wrote: Kahlo splits the canvas into a living side built on complementary colour and a dead side built on greys. The vibration is the argument. Then he sat back. Was he overreaching? He was sixteen and had learned the phrase "complementary colours" eleven minutes ago, and now he was claiming to know what Kahlo intended in 1932. He crossed out "the vibration is the argument" and wrote "the vibration may function as" and hated both versions.

"Found something else," Lane said, leaning over his shoulder with his chin practically on Justin's head, which was Lane's idea of intimacy. "That crack in the ground, all those roots and wires coming out of it. Earthquake stuff. My cousin in Mexico City talks about it, the 85 quake, whole buildings went down. Seismic." He pronounced it with two syllables, like "Sees-mick," and looked enormously pleased with himself.

"The ground is literally broken," Justin said slowly, and the idea began to ferment, the way ideas did when you stopped trying to force them and just let them sit in a warm place. The border itself was the crack. The composition put Kahlo directly on top of it, straddling the fault line, one foot of symbolism in each world, and the plinth made her both a participant and an exhibit, which felt almost too neat except that the painting itself was doing it, right there, in the casserole dish's shadow. He wasn't inventing it. He was, at best, noticing it.

But the dress bothered him. Pink, frilly, folkloric. Was it sincere, or was it a costume worn for the benefit of the grey side, a performance of Mexicanness for a Detroit audience? Ms. Goldberg would call that a reading; the trouble was it was a reading he couldn't prove from the paint alone. The details had a surface truth, a verisimilitude, and behind that surface he honestly couldn't tell what was felt and what was staged, and he suspected Kahlo wouldn't have told him either. He wrote: uncertain whether the dress is claim or costume, and left it in, because Ms. Goldberg had once said the strongest paragraphs in any analysis admit where the evidence runs out.

Lane dropped the tennis ball, finally, and it rolled under the stove. "So. Midnight. Yes or no. Anaelle said she'd save seats but she's not fighting the line alone."

"Give me ten minutes. I'm almost at four hundred words." Justin pulled the legal pad closer and read his last line aloud: "The red blooms against the green as if the ground itself insists on being alive." He could hear Lane already making fun of it, and he could hear the clock, and outside the window a neighbour's dog barked twice at nothing. He said, "Fine. But I'm bringing the pad, and nobody talks during the trailers," and started writing.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Many food banks cannot accept home-cooked or opened food, because they cannot check how it was prepared or stored.
story:
The food bank had overflowed into the library's meeting room again, folding tables pushed against the atlas shelves, and by ten in the morning Lauren was already behind. Ms. Ferreira had given her the sorting job with a warning that the truck from the regional warehouse would come at noon, and whatever wasn't boxed and inventoried by then would not make it onto this week's shelves. Elle and Sahana worked the next table, bagging rice, arguing in the low, comfortable way of people who had argued since seventh grade, while Lauren opened a crate of donated canned goods and tried to decide what counted as good enough.

The trouble arrived at ten forty, in the form of a woman holding a foil pan with a dish towel folded over it like a small blanket. Lauren recognized her before she recognized the dish. The woman lived four doors down from Lauren's house, the one who put out Halloween decorations in September, and she set the pan on the table with the pride of someone presenting a grandchild.

"My lasagna," she said. "The whole one, barely touched. I made it last night thinking of you kids doing this."

Elle looked up. Sahana looked at Lauren. Lauren's hands, which had been sorting black beans, went still.

"Ms. Ferreira," Lauren called, and hated herself a little for it, because she already knew. The orientation sheet, the one she'd skimmed while her mother drove her here, had a line she'd thought was about sour cream tubs and half-eaten cereal. It said the food bank could not accept home-cooked or opened food, because they had no way of checking how it was prepared or stored. She had read it as bureaucracy. Now it had a face and a foil lid.

Ms. Ferreira came over wiping her hands and did it kindly, which somehow made it worse. She thanked the woman twice, said the kitchen must smell wonderful, said the rules were the rules, sorry, it wasn't about her cooking. The woman nodded and picked up the pan and said of course, of course, she understood, and her voice had that particular flatness people use when they understand and don't. She left through the automatic doors by the returns desk, past a cart of donated books where a boy was handing back a glossy volume about Norway, his thumb holding his place on a photograph of a fjord, blue-black water walled in by snow.

"That was brutal," Sahana said, not quietly enough.

"It wasn't," Elle said. "It was the opposite of brutal. It was nice and it still hurt her."

The truck came early, at eleven thirty, and for half an hour there was no time to think. Lauren taped boxes, counted jars of pasta sauce, lugged a bag of lentils that split on the carpet and had to be swept while the driver stood tapping his clipboard. Ms. Ferreira, it turned out, had a system: sealed and labeled went to the shelves, dented but unopened went to a separate table for people to judge for themselves, everything else went back out the door with an apology. It was a sorting, but not a simple one. Lauren had spent the morning trying to dichotomize every item into keep and reject, safe and unsafe, and the lentils on the carpet were proof that the world refused to stay in two piles.

At noon, when the truck was loaded and the room had gone quiet, Sahana found Lauren shelving beans in the far corner. "You know what you are?" Sahana said, dropping cross-legged onto the carpet. "Perspicacious. Word of the day in English. You saw the lasagna coming before she even set it down."

"I saw the rule coming," Lauren said. "I didn't see her."

She was still holding that distinction when a boy from her grade appeared at the intake table with a grocery bag, and Lauren watched Elle take it, glance inside, and look up. Lauren crossed the room. In the bag, under a box of crackers, was a jar of homemade jam with a pressed cloth lid and a strip of masking tape that said, in careful handwriting, Blackberry, Aug.

"It's sealed," the boy said. "My mom boils the jars."

Lauren looked at the tape, at the cloth pressed down under its ring, at the boy's face, which had the same readiness to be generous that the neighbor's had, and she understood that she was going to have to say the sentence herself this time, and that saying it kindly was a skill like any other, one you got better at by doing it badly first.

"We can't take homemade, even sealed," she said. "There's no way for us to check how it was made or stored. I'm sorry. Your mom's blackberries, though." She held the jar up to the window light, where the fruit sat dark and whole. "Take it home and tell her it looked incredible."

The boy almost smiled. Behind him, the line of waiting neighbors stretched toward the fiction section, and Ms. Ferreira was waving Lauren back to the sorting table, where the second truck of the day had just been announced for two o'clock, and the jam went back into the boy's bag, and Lauren went.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that everyone aged 13 to 64 be tested for HIV at least once as part of routine health care.
story:
The condom display was behind the pharmacist's counter, which meant Jake had to ask, which was the entire point of the exercise. Ms. Hoffmann had assigned each of her peer health trainees a "field task" before Saturday's workshop at the community center, and Jake's task was to buy contraception, correctly, out loud, like a person who was not dying. He stood in the aisle between the cough drops and the antacids, rehearsing. Latex. Water-based. Check the expiration date. Behind him a toddler threw a box of bandaids onto the floor with the slow delight of someone who had all day.

He had not expected the pharmacy to smell like this, sharp with rubbing alcohol and something floral from the lotion display, the fluorescent lights buzzing just softly enough to notice once you noticed it. Sahib had drawn the easier assignment, practicing the consent script on a classmate, and had come back to the training room practically glowing. "It's like a knock-knock joke," Sahib had said. "You ask, they answer, and if they don't say who's there, you don't open the door." Jake had written that down, though Ms. Hoffmann would probably call it too cute. She collected epigrams the way other teachers collected late slips, and she had told them on day one that if either of them pontificated at a workshop participant, she would end them. She hadn't specified how.

"Can I help you?" the pharmacist asked. She was older, glasses on a chain, no expression of judgment that Jake could detect, though he checked twice.

"Um. Condoms. A box." His voice cracked on box, which was a gift. "The, uh, latex kind. Water-based lube, if you have it."

She reached without ceremony, slid a box across the counter, and rang it up while Jake read the expiration date twice, because that was the actual assignment, and because his eyes needed something to do. The total came to eleven dollars and change. He paid in coins he had counted at home, which now felt interminable, quarter by quarter, while a man behind him waited with a prescription and infinite patience.

"Doing a school thing?" the pharmacist asked, bagging the box.

"Peer health training. I have to, like, know how to explain this stuff to people." It came out defensive, so he tried again. "I volunteered." That sounded worse. She nodded anyway, merciful, and turned to the next customer.

Outside, Charles-Emile was leaning against the bike rack, holding the clinic pamphlet he'd been assigned to memorize. "You survived," he observed. "Was it terrible?"

"It was eleven dollars and my voice did a thing." Jake sat down on the curb beside him. "How's the clinic stuff?"

Charles-Emile flipped the pamphlet open. "Testing's free at the county clinic, you can walk in, results in about a week, and they don't call your house." He paused. "There's this one part I keep getting wrong, though. About HIV."

Jake took the pamphlet. He'd read the same page the night before, twice, because something in it had surprised him and he'd wanted to be sure. He read it again now, the street noise and the smell of the pharmacy's automatic doors opening and closing behind them, that little exhale of cooled air every ten seconds.

"Okay, so," Jake said, "the CDC recommends everyone aged thirteen to sixty-four gets tested for HIV at least once. Routine. Like, part of regular health care, not because of anything you did."

Charles-Emile squinted at him. "Thirteen?"

"That's what it says. Thirteen to sixty-four, at least once, routine care. I thought you only got tested if, like, something happened. But it's just... a thing they offer everyone." Jake turned the pamphlet over, then back. "Which actually makes it easier to explain to people, because it's not an accusation. It's the same as them checking your blood pressure."

"Huh." Charles-Emile took the pamphlet back. "I've never been tested."

"Me neither."

They sat with that for a minute. Jake looked at the pharmacy bag in his hands and thought about Saturday, about some sixteen-year-old asking him a question he couldn't answer, about the difference between knowing a fact and knowing what to do with it. He could say the recommendation was for everyone thirteen to sixty-four; he could not say why thirteen, or what the counselor at the clinic would ask, or whether he himself would go. Some of it he'd have to learn by walking in.

"My mom's going to find this bag," Charles-Emile said suddenly, "and think it's yours."

"It is mine."

"The pamphlet, I mean."

Jake stood, pulled his bike off the rack. "Want to ride past the clinic? Just to see where the door is."

Charles-Emile folded the pamphlet into his back pocket. "If we're not back by six, my mom calls your mom."

"Then we'll be back by five fifty."

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: In 1824 German historian Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past 'as it actually was', rather than to judge it or instruct the present.
story:
The essay was due Monday, and Alexia had brought it to her aunt's house anyway, folded inside a canvas tote with a jar of her mother's olives. The prompt sat at the top of the page in her own handwriting: Is it possible to describe the past without taking a side? She had underlined "describe" twice, then crossed out the underlining, which left a grey scar across the word.

She set up at the folding table behind the kitchen, where the noise of the gathering could reach her but not swallow her. Her grandfather and his brother were at the counter arguing about the old orchard, the one their father had lost, or traded, or been cheated out of, depending on which of them told it. Her grandfather said the land had been signed away in a single afternoon, a mistake. The brother said their father had known exactly what he was doing, that he had wanted the money for the trip across. Both of them were seventy-some years old, and both spoke as though they had been standing in the room at the time.

"You were four," the brother said.

"I was there," her grandfather said.

Yann arrived with his mother around noon, found Alexia at the folding table, and slid into the chair across from her without asking. He read the prompt upside down, which he could do, and pushed his glasses up.

"Mr. Islam gave us that same question last spring," he said. "I wrote that it's impossible and he wrote 'prove it' in the margin."

"That's helpful."

"He's not a helpful man." Yann took an olive from her jar. "Maddex wrote the opposite, that you just list facts, and Islam marked him down too. So either everyone's wrong or he likes failing people."

Alexia looked past him at her grandfather, who was now drawing the orchard on a napkin, the rows of trees, the gate, the well. The brother drew a different gate. Both men leaned over the napkin, jabbing at it, and Alexia realized that somewhere between their two drawings was a third orchard that had actually existed, and that neither of them had ever seen it, and that no one living had.

"I found something," she said. She turned her notebook around. She'd copied it from the library database two nights before, at the kitchen table, while her mother washed dishes. "In 1824, a German historian named Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past, quote, as it actually was. Not to judge it or instruct the present. He thought you could hold all that other stuff out."

Yann chewed. "In 1824. So a German guy almost two hundred years ago thought you could just show it."

"As it actually was," Alexia said. "Those are his words. That's the whole point of them."

"And nobody's argued with him since?"

"Everybody's argued with him since." She hadn't written that yet. She'd only just understood it, sitting here between two versions of an orchard. "But that's the thing. He's the reason the question exists. Before him, people mostly wrote history to teach lessons. He said, no, stop. Just show it."

Maddex came through the kitchen then with a plate of cake, having followed the smell, and put the plate down on Alexia's notebook before she could stop him. "Whose history essay? Yours? What's it on?"

"The orchard," she said, and surprised herself.

Maddex looked at the two old men, still bent over the napkin, still arguing about a gate. "The one the great-grandfather lost?"

"Traded," Yann said.

"Lost," said Maddex, because that was the version everyone in his family told.

Alexia lifted the plate off her notebook. There was a smear of icing across her margin, which was, she thought, exactly what happened to every source sooner or later, a thumbprint here, a grudge there, the whole alluvial record silting up with whatever the teller happened to be standing in. She thought about her grandfather's version, how it had calcified over sixty years of telling until it was less a memory than a monument, something you visited, something with a fixed shape. She would never get the orchard back. That much was certain. What she might get, if she asked both men the same questions in the same order and wrote down both answers, was the shape of the disagreement itself, which was a kind of truth, though not the kind Ranke had promised.

She left the table and went to the counter, notebook under her arm. "What was the gate made of?" she asked.

Both men stopped. Her grandfather said wood. The brother said iron, and that it had squealed when you pushed it, and that our father could not stand the sound of it, and that this was why he had wanted to leave, and her grandfather went quiet in a way she had never seen, and said, "He never told me that."

"Where would he tell you it," the brother said. "You were a child."

"I was there," her grandfather said again, but softer, and this time it sounded less like a claim and more like a wound, and Alexia wrote down both gates, and under them: wood/iron, and left the rest of the line empty.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Keeping money as cash has an opportunity cost: the interest or returns it could have earned in a savings account or investment.
story:
The envelope of cash had lived in the back of Kaylee's sock drawer since September, four hundred and sixty dollars in twenties and fives, the whole amount earned at the greenhouse on Saturdays. She had been saving toward the senior trip deposit, two hundred dollars due to Mr. Navarro by Friday, and she had been telling herself for months that keeping the money where she could see it was the responsible thing. On Tuesday morning she carried the envelope to school in her backpack, because the deposit window in the main office opened at lunch, and she intended to pay in person.

She found Ian in the chemistry hallway before first period, slumped against the radiator with the morose expression he wore whenever the swim coach posted times. He had driven to the dealership on Saturday with his father, he said, and stood in the lot beside a gray Civic with a crease in the rear fender, cash from his graduation cards folded in his pocket. His father had asked the salesman whether it made sense to pay cash for the whole thing, and the salesman had said something that Ian was still turning over.

"He said keeping money as cash has an opportunity cost," Ian told her. "The interest or returns it could have earned in a savings account or an investment. That's the whole sentence. Then he tried to sell my dad an extended warranty."

Kaylee turned the sentence over too, all through second period, while the sub requisitioned a projector that never arrived and the class watched a video about buffer solutions. She thought about her own envelope. The credit union two blocks from school had a savings account, her mother had mentioned it once, the kind that paid interest. Four hundred and sixty dollars sitting in a sock drawer earned nothing at all, and would earn nothing until she spent it, and every month it sat there was a month of interest she would never see. That was the cost of being able to see it. She wrote the words next to her chemistry notes: next best alternative, the thing you give up.

At lunch she went to the office anyway, because the trip was the whole point of saving, and stood in line behind Maurice, who was paying his deposit with a card. When her turn came she set the envelope on the counter and then, without quite deciding to, pulled it back. She asked the secretary whether the deposit could wait until Thursday. The secretary said Friday was the deadline, and Thursday was fine, and Kaylee walked out of the office with the envelope still in her hand, feeling both clever and slightly sick.

She spent Thursday morning thinking it through, and by noon she had assembled a position she could defend. Some of the money, the two hundred for the deposit, was money she had already chosen to spend; holding it one more day earned her nothing but a single day of interest, which was nearly nothing, and that was fine. The rest, the two hundred and sixty that would keep growing until graduation, was the part that had been sitting still by her own volition, and stillness, she now understood, was not the same as safety. She wanted both things at once, the certainty of cash and the slow arithmetic of an account, and she could not have both, because that was what choosing meant.

After school she walked to the credit union with Maurice, who came along because he wanted a lollipop from the bowl by the teller window and had no better errand. The account took eleven minutes to open. She kept sixty in the envelope, which she told Maurice was for gas money and which was really for the feeling of it, the paper, the drawer, the proof she could touch. The rest went into the account, and the teller showed her a screen with a small number on it that would get slightly larger on its own.

Then came the twist, and it arrived quietly, the way things did in that town. On Friday morning Mr. Navarro announced over the intercom that the senior trip fund had been oversubscribed and that anyone who paid by the end of the day would be charged the original two hundred, while later payments would go up to two hundred and forty. Kaylee heard it in the courtyard with her sandwich halfway to her mouth. She had two hundred and sixty dollars in an account now, and sixty in the envelope, and a deposit due by three o'clock, and the account, it turned out, could not be drawn from until the hold cleared on Monday.

She solved it the way problems in that town got solved, by walking. She went to the office at two forty, handed over the sixty from the envelope, and asked the secretary if she could owe the rest until Monday, when the hold lifted. Mr. Navarro happened to be in the office arguing about the bus requisition form, and he looked up and said, "Monday's fine, Kaylee, put the form in my box." She wrote her name, the amount, the date, and slid the form into the wooden box with the little brass label that said nothing at all about interest.

She walked back out to the courtyard with the envelope lighter and the deposit half paid, and found Ian still morose by the fence, still thinking about the Civic. She sat down next to him and said, "So what did your dad do in the end?" Ian shrugged and turned his phone toward her, showing a photo of the gray car parked in their driveway.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: In countries with low death rates, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman is needed to replace the population without migration.
story:
The dashboard said 214 kilometres to the coast, and Maika had already eaten both bags of trail mix before the town limits disappeared in the mirror. Keira sat folded into the back seat with Mr. Nolan's old demography workbook open on her knees, because Mr. Nolan, who was taciturn by nature and monosyllabic by July, had offered her a deal: if she could teach the unit back to him in September, she could skip the exam. She had said yes mostly to see his face do something, and it had, briefly, like a window opening an inch in a sealed house.

"I still don't get it," Emiliano said from the driver's seat, glancing at her in the mirror the way he glanced at everything, sideways and amused. "You've read that page four times. It's a triangle with stripes. My little brother draws those."

"It's a population pyramid," Keira said, with the caution of someone testing ice. "Bars for each age group. Wide base means lots of kids. Fat middle means the country got busy a few decades ago." She turned the workbook toward the window so the light caught the printed chart, a narrow, top-heavy shape like an onion balanced on its tip. "This one's Japan, sort of. Old on top, thin at the bottom. You look at it and you can guess whether the country needs to build schools or nursing homes."

Emiliano's want, which he had announced before they left and defended twice at gas stations, was to reach the coast by sunset so he could photograph the lighthouse in what he called the correct light. Maika's want was quieter and stranger: she wanted to run the whole trip without once consulting her phone, a self-imposed rule she enforced with the rectitude of a customs officer, so that when Emiliano asked about a turnoff she would only say, "The paper map says left, and I believe the paper map."

The argument that followed, about whether the paper map was older than the road itself, carried them past a shuttered creamery and a field of sunflowers all facing the wrong way, and Keira barely heard it. She was stuck on one number. The workbook said her own country's fertility rate had slipped below 2.1, and it called that figure replacement level, and she could not make it sit still in her head. She was eighteen and had done calculus; she knew that two parents having two children should, in a tidy world, exactly replace themselves.

"Okay, question," she said, interrupting a dispute about whether sunflowers followed the sun or ran from it. "If every couple has exactly two kids, why isn't the population steady? Why does the book say you need 2.1?"

"Because books lie," Maika said serenely, studying the map.

"Because some kids grow up to be lighthouse photographers," Emiliano said, "and that's basically not reproducing."

"Ha. But seriously. Two for two. It should balance." She said it and then heard it, the way you hear a wrong note only after it has left the piano. The workbook had not explained, and it occurred to her that Mr. Nolan's deal was not really about the unit. It was about whether she could sit with a number that refused to be simple, whether she could hold two things at once: the tidy version she wanted to be true and the actual figure, 2.1, replacement level, in countries where not many people die young. She flipped pages, looking for the clean paragraph that would settle it, and found instead a different pyramid, a wide-based one, a country drowning in children and building schools everywhere.

"So some countries can't build classrooms fast enough," she said slowly, "and others are looking at their skinny little base and realizing the schools will empty out and they'll need nursing homes instead. Same chart. Two futures. And the 2.1, whether you like it or not, is the line between them." Emiliano whooped, not because of demography but because the lighthouse had appeared on the horizon, a white needle against the going-gold sky, and he began hunting for a turn lane with the urgency of a man late for an appointment with light.

They parked on gravel and tumbled out, and Emiliano crouched with his camera, and Maika stood very straight beside the paper map as though it had enfranchised her to vote on the whole coastline. Keira took the workbook with her, held it open against the wind, and looked from the chart to the horizon. She did not know yet why 2.1 and not 2, and she decided, in the honest part of herself where Mr. Nolan apparently lived, that she would tell him exactly that in September: here is what the pyramid says, here is what I know, and here is the small stubborn gap where the number does something I can't yet follow.

"Get in the shot," Emiliano called. "Keira. The light's dying. Bring the triangle."

"It's a pyramid," she said, but she ran toward him anyway, book flapping like a bird.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed, so doubling a car's speed makes the distance needed to brake about four times as long.
story:
Justin's hands were at ten and two, exactly where Ms. Villanueva had put them, and the family car smelled like his mother's coffee and the pine tree air freshener that had died sometime last winter. "Turn out of the lot," Ms. Villanueva said. She was a neighbor who had taught half the kids on their street, a phlegmatic woman who never raised her voice and never seemed to need to. "Then straight down Corbett until I tell you otherwise." The road was empty and the afternoon light came in low and yellow, and the permit in Justin's pocket was eight days old.

He wanted this lesson over with by five, because Marianne and Reese had texted that they were meeting at the quarry at five thirty and he wanted to be the one who drove there, not the one who got dropped off. That was the whole plan: pass the road test in three weeks, borrow the car, arrive under his own power. Marianne had already promised to abrogate the seating chart they'd used since sophomore year, the one where Justin always rode in the middle of the back seat, if he showed up behind the wheel.

"Ease up to twenty," Ms. Villanueva said. He did it, and the car felt like a living thing cooperating with him for the first time. "Now brake gently, come to a full stop at that mail truck." He stopped a car length short of it, pleased with himself.

"Good," she said. "Now I want you to guess something. Same car, same road, but at forty instead of twenty. How many times longer do you need to stop?" Justin looked at the speedometer as if it owed him the answer. "Double," he said. "Twice the speed, twice the room." It felt like arithmetic he could trust, clean and obvious.

Ms. Villanueva didn't confirm or deny. She had this way of withholding approval that Justin found unnerving, as if the veracity of every claim had to be tested before it earned her attention. "Get up to forty on the straight stretch," she said. "There's a stop sign at Fenwick. Start braking when you normally would from twenty." The stretch unrolled ahead of him, and he accelerated, and the road began to move past faster than his stomach expected.

He began braking where felt right, at the same mailbox he'd judged before, and the stop sign came at him like it had opinions. He pressed harder, the seatbelt bit his chest, the tires held but the car kept traveling, traveling, and he stopped with the sign beside his window instead of in front of his bumper. His hands were damp on the wheel. Ms. Villanueva said nothing for a moment, which was somehow louder than the engine.

"Four," Justin said finally. "It's four times as long, isn't it. Doubling the speed makes the stopping distance about four times what it was." He had gotten it wrong out loud and now he had gotten it right out loud, and neither one had required her to say a word. "That's why the sign came at me like that." She nodded once. "Again," she said. "Forty, and this time pick your braking point knowing what you know." He turned around at the next intersection and came back, and this time he started braking far earlier than every instinct told him to, and the car settled to a stop with room to spare, smooth as a held breath.

They were running short on the hour, the quarry deadline pressing in, and when they pulled back into the lot Reese was already leaning against the mailbox at the corner of the street, hood up, checking his phone. "Same time Thursday," Ms. Villanueva said, unbuckling. "You'll want to practice the math until it lives in your foot, not your head." Justin pulled out his phone to text Marianne that he'd be late, then stopped, watching Reese across the street. Three weeks until the test, and he had learned something today that doubled back on itself and made everything four times bigger than he'd assumed. He honked once, short, and Reese looked up and grinned and started walking toward the car.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, elevated blood pressure means a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic reading below 80.
story:
Vincent sat in the dentist's waiting room with his mother's phone in his hand, staring at the number the pharmacy machine had printed an hour before: 125 over 78. She was in the chair now, behind the door with the frosted window, getting a crown replaced, and she had handed him the slip of paper in the parking lot with the flat instruction to figure out whether it meant anything.

He had told her it probably meant nothing. She had said, "You're the one applying to health sciences," and gone inside.

The waiting room smelled of mint and hot plastic. A television above the reception desk played a loop about gum disease with the sound off. Vincent typed "125 over 78" into the search bar, then deleted it, because typing a parent's numbers into a phone felt like reading her mail. He typed it again.

The results came back in layers. Some sites used an older system where anything under 140 over 90 counted as normal, and those sites made 125 sound like nothing at all. Others used a 2017 American guideline, and under that one the landscape shifted. Normal, the table said, was systolic under 120 and diastolic under 80. Then there was a category above normal, before anything called hypertension began, and it had a specific boundary: elevated blood pressure meant a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic reading below 80. Below 130, above 119, and the diastolic still in the safe zone. He read the row twice, moving his finger along it on the screen. His mother's numbers sat inside it, both of them, 125 and 78.

He thought of Brennan, who had a gift for making serious things sound like jokes. Last spring, in the cafeteria, Brennan had read a headline about sodium limits aloud in a facetious news-anchor voice, and half the table had laughed, and Vincent had laughed too, and then had gone home and eaten the same fries. Now he wondered whether the joke had been the whole of what any of them took from it. He could hear Brennan saying "elevated," with the vowels stretched out, and he could hear Cael, who never stretched anything, saying that a single reading in a pharmacy meant nothing because machines in pharmacies were wrong half the time.

Both of those were true in their ways. That was the problem. Vincent had spent two years learning to argue one side of a question cleanly, for debate club, for essays, for the applications he was drafting in a notebook at home. He was good at holding a position until the round ended. He was less practiced at holding two positions at once and refusing to collapse either one.

The dental hygienist came out and told him his mother needed ten more minutes. He asked if he could use the corner where the old blood pressure cuff sat on a stand, the kind with the dial, and she said, "Go ahead, it's sanitized," in a tone that suggested he was the first person to ask all year. He wrapped the cuff around his own arm, pumped it, and watched the needle shudder. His own reading came out 118 over 74. He tried it again on the other arm. 116 over 76. He wrote both on the back of the pharmacy slip, next to his mother's numbers, then drew a small table with three columns: hers, his, the guideline's boundary. The columns made the fact quieter somehow. It stopped being a verdict and became a coordinate.

He texted Cael a photo of the table. Cael replied within a minute: "so it's called elevated. not high. there's a difference?" Vincent typed back, "Under the 2017 American guideline, elevated means systolic 120 to 129 with diastolic below 80." Cael sent back a thumbs up and then, separately, "my dad's was 160 for years and he's fine," which was exactly the kind of evidence that meant everything and nothing.

The receptionist called his mother's name for checkout. She came out pressing gauze to her jaw, signed the card, and took her keys from Vincent. In the car, before starting the engine, she looked at the slip he handed back to her, with his table on the reverse.

"What's the verdict?" she said.

"There isn't one," Vincent said. "It's called elevated. Under the guideline they use now, that's systolic 120 to 129 with the bottom number still under 80. It's under 125 for you. It's not high. It's not nothing."

"That's a very diplomatic answer."

"It's the accurate answer." He hesitated. "There's stuff about walking and less salt that goes with it. I can read it to you if you want. Or not."

She put the slip in the cupholder and pulled out of the parking space. At the first red light she reached over and turned the slip so the table faced her, and read it with her finger, the way he had.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: The Heckscher-Ohlin model, named after Swedish economists Eli Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin, explains comparative advantage by differences in countries' supplies of land, labor and capital.
story:
Ella had set the lemonade stand up at the end of Ms. Li's driveway because Ms. Li had the only table, and she was telling everyone who stopped that she understood comparative advantage completely, which was not entirely true, though she believed it every time she said it. She had a pitcher, a cash box that Lennon had lent her without asking what it was for, and a textbook open on the corner of the table, weighted down with a rock because the afternoon wind kept flipping it to the chapter on taxes, which she had definitely not read.

"Say it back to me," she said when Benoit arrived, hands in his pockets, suspicious of the whole operation. "You're a country. I'm a country."

"I'm a country," Benoit said. "Which one."

"Doesn't matter. I can make lemonade and I can make iced tea, and you can make both too, but I'm better at lemonade and you're better at tea, and so if we each do the thing we're relatively better at and trade, we both end up with more of both." She poured him a cup he hadn't paid for, which undercut her economics somewhat, and he drank it anyway.

"Then why does the book have a whole chapter on Sweden," Benoit said, and turned the rock aside and flipped the pages with one thumb. He read slower than she wanted him to. "It says Heckscher-Ohlin."

"Named after Eli Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin," Lennon said, arriving from the direction of her own house with a jar of ice, as if she had been listening from across the street, which she probably had. "They were Swedish economists. My brother took this course last year and complained about it at dinner for a semester."

Ella took the book back and found the paragraph, and the paragraph said the thing that made the afternoon interesting: that comparative advantage wasn't only about who was better at what, but about what countries had a lot of. The Heckscher-Ohlin model explained it by differences in countries' supplies of land, labor and capital. She read it twice, and the second time a question assembled itself, the kind she liked, the kind that felt like a door left ajar.

"So it's not about skill," she said slowly. "Or not only. A country with vast farmland exports grain not because its farmers are geniuses but because land is what it has the most of. And a country full of factories and money imports the grain and sends back electronics." She looked at the stand as if seeing it for the first time. "We're not even selling lemonade. We're selling the fact that my driveway has shade and a table and yours doesn't."

Ms. Li came out at four with an empty glass and a distant, ascetic expression that Ella had privately decided was the look of someone who had given up dessert for a year. She paid for two glasses and stood listening, the way neighbors do, half in the conversation and half in her own afternoon.

"What I don't understand," Ella told her, because she had decided, on reflection, that honesty was cheaper than confidence, "is whether trade makes the countries more alike or keeps them different. Like, is it a good thing that the farmland country stays the farmland country? Every stratum of the textbook says both countries gain, and I believe it, but the grain country is still the grain country. That part they don't say."

"They don't," Ms. Li agreed, and drank her lemonade, and offered nothing further, which was either cruelty or wisdom.

"I think I'm going to write my essay about that," Ella said, and it came out more certain than she felt, because she had a habit of aggrandizing small understandings into large ones, and somewhere she knew this. Maybe the essay would be about how both things could be true at once, the gains and the sameness. Maybe it would be shorter than that and mostly questions. Lennon was already stacking cups, and Benoit had claimed the iced tea as his comparative advantage and was pouring it wrong, too much sugar, a thick amber stratum at the bottom of each glass that no amount of stirring would fix.

"Country," Ella said, and held out the pitcher, "you want to trade?"

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Blocking is the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals.
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and old velvet, and Alexandra had claimed it for three hours every Tuesday with a sign-up sheet that Mr. Campbell had initialed without much hope. She was sixteen and had never directed anything, but she had watched the fall musical from the lighting booth four nights running, taking notes in a green spiral book, and she had decided that what she wanted was not to be watched but to arrange the watching. Now she stood on the stage with six actors holding photocopied scripts, and the one-act she had chosen, twenty minutes about three siblings dividing a dead mother's kitchen, refused to sit still in her head.

"Scene one, you're all at the table," she said. "That part I can see." The problem was scene two, where the siblings scatter through the house arguing, and by the second run-through Martina and Maia had collided twice behind the prop refrigerator, once hard enough that Maia dropped a plastic colander and laughed the kind of laugh that covers being startled. Alexandra stopped the run and pressed her pencil against her lip. She had read the word in a library book about directing, between a chapter on tablework and a chapter on tempo, and she thought she finally understood it as a thing you made rather than a thing you found.

"Okay," she said. "We're going to set the blocking." Martina looked at her with her chin tipped, the way she did when she suspected vocabulary was being used against her. "Blocking is the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage," Alexandra said. "I set it, in rehearsal. So it's mine to get wrong, not yours." Maia grinned, and something in the room loosened, because a plan that belonged to someone else was apparently easier to bump into than a plan that belonged to everyone.

They worked it a line at a time. Alexandra walked the diagonal herself, counting steps, then had Maia cross on the cue about the good knives, and Martina take the window on the cue about the garden, and the near-collision dissolved into two clean paths. She discovered she had opinions she hadn't known she held: that grief moved in straight lines, that the youngest sibling should always be the one left alone upstage. Mr. Campbell came in near the end, sat in the third row with his coat still on, and said only, "Sightlines on the left, when she kneels," and went back to his newspaper, and Alexandra marked it in the green book without impugning his brief attention, because a note given briefly was still a note given.

What she could not resolve was the last page. The script wanted the three siblings to stand in a row facing the audience and say nothing for eight seconds, and Alexandra, who had privately suspected for years that she was a bit of an aesthete, loved the image coldly, the way she loved certain photographs. But Maia had said, quietly, on their way out, that standing still that long made her feel like an exhibit, that it was too somatic, that her body wanted somewhere to go and the script refused it. Alexandra had said she'd think about it, and she had, for four days, and the thinking had not closed.

It was Martina who noticed the trouble had a second layer.
