She had come early on Tuesday to sweep the stage, which she did without being asked, broom strokes slow and even, because sweeping was what she did instead of being nervous. Martina wanted the brother's role, the one currently held by a boy who kept checking his phone between runs, and she had wanted it since the auditions, and she had said nothing about it for three weeks. When Alexandra arrived, scripts under her arm, Martina leaned on the broom and said, "If he's late again, put me on as the brother for one run. Just to see the shape of it."

They saw the shape of it. Martina read the brother with her chin down and her hands busy, and the row of siblings at the end became something Alexandra hadn't planned: a line of people standing apart together, each holding a different stillness. Maia, watching from the wings, said nothing, then walked out and took her mark and said, "I can do the eight seconds if she's next to me. It's different when it's not just me standing there."

Alexandra stood in the fifth row with her pencil going, and did not write anything yet. The cold image she had loved was still in the script, but it had changed owners somewhere in the rehearsal, and she could not tell whether that was a failure of her eye or the whole point of directing, and she suspected she would not know until an audience sat where she was sitting. The real cast list, the phone-checking boy, the audition Martina had never mentioned again: all of it waited outside the auditorium doors.

"All right," she said, walking back toward the stage. "From the top of scene two. And Martina, keep the broom handy."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Jordyn arrived at the Vista twelve minutes early, which she decided was nine minutes too many, so she walked to the concession counter and back twice, pretending to study the candy like a person with real intentions. The theater smelled of melted butter and the particular cold dust of old carpet. When Keven came through the doors with his jacket half-zipped over a shirt she suspected he had agonized over, she was holding the popcorn she had bought mostly so her hands would have a job.

"You got the tickets already," he said. It wasn't quite a question.

"Mr. Katz waved me through. He takes tickets on Fridays now. He said we'd better not sit in the back row like his nephew does." Mr. Katz, retired from teaching biology, had taken one look at the two of them and smiled in a way Jordyn found both warm and slightly humiliating.

They found seats in the middle, and for the first twenty minutes of the movie the popcorn traveled between them like a small diplomatic offering, a rapprochement conducted one kernel at a time. She kept losing the plot. There was a spy, or possibly a double agent, and every time Keven laughed she matched it half a second late, like badly dubbed film.

Afterward, outside under the marquee's buzzing light, the trouble started. She'd meant to say the movie was clever, but what came out was "It was long," which sounded peevish even to her, the complaint of someone who had not just spent two hours in a dark room next to a boy she liked. Keven looked at the sidewalk. Then he looked at the schedule printed by the door and said the seven o'clock showing was shorter, if she ever wanted to see the same movie again but faster. She couldn't tell whether that was a joke or an invitation, so she said "ha" in a tone that committed to neither.

They walked to her corner. He kicked a bottle cap the length of a block, narrating its progress like a sportscaster, and she laughed for real, but she filed the earlier moment away, and by the time she was unlocking her door she was replaying everything: the "ha," the "long," the way she had transliterated her actual feelings into whatever "ha" was in the language of people who are smooth. It was obvious, she concluded, standing in the kitchen eating the leftover popcorn cold, that he had endured the evening the way you endure a dentist.

At school Monday, Hailey cornered her by the lockers. "So? Scale of one to disaster."

"He was nice," Jordyn said. "It was fine."

Hailey squinted. Across the hall, Keven was telling something to a group and had not looked over once, which Jordyn took as evidence. She had a whole case built by lunch: no text Saturday, no text Sunday, the schedule remark, the kicked bottle cap as compensation for boredom. She laid it out for Hailey in the courtyard, and Hailey ate her chips and listened, which was generous of her.

"Okay," Hailey said finally, "except." She turned her phone around. Keven had sent her a message that morning, asking whether Jordyn had said anything about Saturday, because he was pretty sure he had ruined it by talking through the previews, and could she find out, without making it obvious, whether Jordyn would want to try again. "Keven quotes things at me sometimes," Hailey said, scrolling. "Last week it was this thing, a 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues. They found a liking gap. After a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company." She pocketed the phone. "He sent me that Saturday night at eleven."

Jordyn stood very still, holding her own conviction up to the light and watching it go crooked. Hailey asked what she wanted to do about it. Jordyn said nothing, then took out her phone and typed, deleted, and typed again, and finally sent him a message about the seven o'clock showing. She hit send before she could file the moment away for later regret, and stood in the courtyard listening for the buzz.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The molar mass of a compound is the sum of the molar masses of the atoms in its formula; for carbon dioxide it is 12.01 plus two times 16.00, or 44.01 grams per mole.
story:
The kitchen smelled of cardamom because her mother was boiling milk for tea, and Vanessa spread her chemistry homework across the table as though claiming territory. Next to the saucepan, between the sugar bowl and a stack of unopened mail, she laid out the worksheet, her calculator, and the index card Sage had made her in the library two days ago. The card said, in Sage's round looping handwriting, molar mass is your bridge. Vanessa had liked that then. Now, alone with the numbers, she found the bridge had no visible far side.

The problem wanted grams of carbon dioxide produced from a given mass of reactant, and the first step, according to the worksheet, was to find the molar mass of carbon dioxide. Vanessa looked up the atomic masses on the table Mr. Tran had distributed in class: carbon, 12.01; oxygen, 16.00. She wrote 12.01 plus 16.00 on the back of her hand, added them, and got 28.01. She carried that number forward through the division, the mole ratio, the multiplication, and arrived at an answer that felt heavy in a way she couldn't name. Her phone buzzed on the counter.

Tyra had sent a photograph of her own work, which was a Tyra move, less a request for help than a demonstration that help would be unnecessary. Vanessa enlarged the image. At the top, in Tyra's angular print, was the figure 44.01 grams per mole, and beside it the line two oxygens, obviously. Vanessa looked at her own hand. The formula was CO2. The little two. She had known the two was there the way she knew her grandmother's birthday, a fact kept rather than used. She remembered, suddenly, her grandmother's kitchen two summers ago, the morning the old woman made her weigh flour for a cake and refused to give the measurement in cups. A scale does not lie, her grandmother had said, tapping the bowl. Twice as much flour is twice as much cake. Vanessa had thought this was a lecture; now it seemed closer to a gift.

She wrote the calculation again, this time as 12.01 plus two times 16.00, and watched the number assemble itself, 44.01, the same figure Tyra had, arrived at by a different road. The rest of the problem reorganized itself around the correction, and the answer that emerged was smaller than her first one and, she thought, more plausible, though she could not have said why plausibility was something an answer could have. She texted Tyra a photograph of her work with no caption, an admission and a counterclaim at once.

Her mother set a cup of tea down beside the calculator and looked over her shoulder without asking. When Vanessa was eleven, her mother used to check her arithmetic every night, standing at the kitchen table with a red pen, and Vanessa had borne it the way she then bore everything, gratefully and with resentment arriving later, in private. By thirteen she had asked her to stop, and her mother had stopped that same evening, without argument, which had felt like winning and also, strangely, like being left. Now her mother said only, "Is that the same stuff Mr. Tran pontificates about on Back to School Night?" and Vanessa said, "He doesn't pontificate, he's just thorough," and found she meant it, mostly.

Tyra replied with a single word, correct, and then a second message: how did you get it. Vanessa considered lying. There was a version of herself, well established at school, who treated every right answer as native property, and that self had a certain social standing to maintain, one that Sage, who wrote bridges on index cards, did not benefit from and did not seem to miss. But Tyra had asked directly, and the question sat in the message window like a coin on a counter. Vanessa typed: I forgot to double the oxygen the first time. 44.01 is 12.01 plus two times 16.00. I got 28.01 and it was wrong. She stared at the sentence. It cost something to send, and she sent it anyway, and the cost turned out to be smaller than she had estimated, which was its own kind of calculation.

She was aware, in the quiet that followed, that the honest thing and the useful thing had pointed the same direction this once, and that they would not always. Sage would say the truth was an absolute; Tyra would call that naive and probably say something about primogeniture, the way she did whenever they argued about inheritance in the novels for English class, firstborns taking everything while younger siblings made themselves ancillary. Vanessa held both positions the way she now held the two atomic masses, one in each hand, not equal, not resolved, and did not pretend they balanced. Tyra's reply came: oh, I did that on the quiz last month. Vanessa laughed out loud, alone in the kitchen, and her mother glanced over.

She copied the corrected solution onto a fresh sheet in her best handwriting, boxed the answer, and wrote 44.01 grams per mole at the top of the page where she would see it first tomorrow. Then she turned the index card over and added, beneath Sage's bridge, a second line in her own smaller print: check the little numbers too. She slid the card into her backpack's front pocket, zipped it, and picked up the tea, which had gone lukewarm while she worked. Her mother was already at the sink, washing the saucepan, and Vanessa carried her cup over to stand beside her and said, "Twice as much flour is twice as much cake. Did Grandma ever tell you that?"

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Carryover cooking means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests.
story:
The roast had been on the rotisserie since five, and Aaron had been telling everyone at the party that he knew exactly what he was doing. His mother was inside with the aunts, his father was pretending to supervise from a folding chair, and the backyard had filled with people Aaron half knew, cousins and neighbours, all of them drifting toward the smoke the way animals drift toward water on one of those nature programs, the yard suddenly a small savanna of folding tables and paper plates. He had a thermometer in his hand and a number in his head, one hundred thirty-five, medium rare, and when the display flashed the number at 6:40 he announced it to the yard like a referee.

"Perfect timing," he said, and he meant it, and he took the roast off the spit himself, no help, carried it to the cutting board near the fence with both hands and a dish towel.

Mr. Jean-Louis was leaning on the fence that separated the two yards, as he had been all evening, holding a cup of something and watching with an expression Aaron couldn't read. Aaron wanted to read it as admiration. He'd decided weeks ago, though he'd never said it aloud, that this meal was partly for Mr. Jean-Louis, who had lived next door since Aaron was six, who had watched him fall off that same fence and get back up, and who had, Aaron believed, once told him he cooked like somebody's grandmother. Though when he tried to remember when that had been said, or whether it had been said at all, the memory wouldn't come clean.

"You taking it off now?" Mr. Jean-Louis asked. Not a judgment, just a question.

"At one thirty-five," Aaron said. "That's the number."

Mr. Jean-Louis nodded slowly, the way he nodded at most things, and sipped his cup, and said nothing else, and Aaron chose to find this reassuring rather than otherwise.

Oscar arrived late, the way he always did, apologizing with a six-pack and a story about traffic that Aaron didn't believe, because Oscar had never once in his life been stopped by traffic, only by his own decision to leave the house when he felt like it. Oscar was a year into some program downtown, taking night classes, talking about the city as if it had personally chosen him, calling it cosmopolitan, a word he'd started using that Aaron privately found exhausting. Oscar looked at the roast on the board, glistening and tented under foil, and said it looked like something from a restaurant, and Aaron felt the evening gathering itself around him, everything he'd planned arriving on schedule.

Then he cut into it at seven, ten minutes before his mother called everyone to eat, and the centre was grey.

Not blackened, not ruined, but grey all the way through, the pink gone from it, and Aaron stood over the board with the knife in his hand and felt the specific vertigo of having done everything right and gotten everything wrong. He checked the thermometer against his palm. It read ninety-something. He checked the notes on his phone, where he'd written one thirty-five in his own handwriting. He had, he was almost certain, pulled it at exactly the number. Almost certain. There was a version of the evening in which he'd glanced at the display, seen a three, assumed the rest. He couldn't rule that version out, and he hated that he couldn't.

"You pulled it right on target, didn't you," Mr. Jean-Louis said over the fence, and it wasn't a question this time. "Carryover cooking," he said, and left it at that, turning back toward his own dark kitchen, cup in hand.

Aaron stood there turning the phrase over. Carryover. The roast had kept going after he'd stopped it, had finished without him, and there was nothing to be done now except carry the platter to the table and let people eat it, which they did, and praised it, his aunts eulogizing his grandmother's Sunday roasts as they always did whenever anyone cooked anything, his father going back for seconds, Oscar taking a picture of his plate for people Aaron would never meet.

His mother caught his eye across the table and raised her glass an inch, and he raised his back. Later, after dark, when the yard had emptied and the savanna of tables stood bare, Aaron washed the thermometer under the hose spigot and thought about next time, about pulling it early, at a number he'd have to guess, some subtraction he didn't yet know how to do. Or he could ask Mr. Jean-Louis, tomorrow, over the fence. He looked at the lit window of the neighbour's kitchen, then at the foil still crumpled on the cutting board, still faintly warm.

"One thirty next time," he said to the yard, and screwed the hose shut.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees.
story:
The potato salad had been on the picnic table since noon, and it was now a quarter past eight, and Christian stood over it in the family kitchen with a wooden spoon in one hand and his phone in the other, doing arithmetic he distrusted. He was sixteen and had volunteered to handle the leftovers, mostly because his mother had said "you're the responsible one," which he suspected was less a compliment than a delegation of blame. The counter was a wreck of foil trays and half-eaten buns, and the kitchen smelled like charcoal and miracle whip.

He texted Daniel first, because Daniel's family did cookouts constantly and Daniel had opinions about everything. "how long can potato salad sit out before it kills us," he typed. "asking for the salad." Daniel replied with a shrugging emoji and then, usefully, a link. Christian read it twice, frowning at his phone. Perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or for more than one hour when the air is above 90 degrees.

"Great," Christian said to the potato salad. "So which was it today?" He had a vague memory of the thermometer on the porch railing reading 88 around lunch, and a clearer memory of his uncle complaining, around four, that it felt like the surface of the sun. Four o'clock. Six and a quarter hours ago. Whatever the exact air temperature had done, the salad had lost.

He checked the fridge thermometer out of a new sense of duty: 38 degrees, safely under 40, which meant the cold side of the rule was being honored in this house at least retroactively. The burgers were fine, having stayed in the cooler with ice until the end. The devilled eggs were borderline; Maia had brought them out at one, but her father had kept the platter shaded and Christian had seen him swap it for a cold one at some point, though he could not have sworn to the time. That was the problem with a rule built on hours and degrees: it demanded a witness with a stopwatch, and all Christian had was a day that had run together like mayonnaise.

He called Maia, who answered out of breath from something, probably her own family's cookout, everyone having one apparently, a holiday mandated by the weather.

"Did your dad swap the egg platter?" he asked.

"Christian," Maia said. "What a question. Yes, twice. He's obsessive about it. He took the old one back inside around two, I think. Why, are you deciding what survives?"

"Basically. If stuff sat between 40 and 140 degrees for more than two hours, it's out. And if it was over 90 outside, you only get one hour."

"Look at you with your food safety pragmatics," Maia said. "Very butch. Keep the eggs, obviously. My father has never once poisoned a guest, though he has bored several."

He laughed and hung up and stood there with the spoon, and for a second he did introspect, which was not a thing he usually admitted to, about how odd it was that he cared. Yesterday he would have scraped everything into containers and hoped. But the rule had changed the shape of the decision: it was no longer "is this probably fine," which was tautological anyway, since fine food is food that is fine, and it had become something countable. Two hours, or one if it was hot. He liked countable. He also distrusted it, since he could not actually reconstruct the day in clean hours. The certainty of the rule met the fog of the afternoon and the fog won on details.

Mr. Krause, the neighbour, chose that moment to appear at the back door holding the borrowed serving spoon from the coleslaw, which had crossed the fence in a transaction Christian had not witnessed. "Everything all right in here?" Mr. Krause asked. "Heard you talking to someone about poison."

"Maia," Christian said. "About eggs." He held up his phone with the guidance on it. "Perishables shouldn't be out more than two hours between 40 and 140 degrees. One hour if it's over 90 out. So I'm triaging."

Mr. Krause peered at the screen, then at the counter, and delivered his verdict with the gravity of a man judging a pie contest. "The potato salad's a garrison, son. The coleslaw rode home in my cooler, it lives. The eggs are a coin flip."

"That's what Maia said, except the coin part," Christian said. He picked up the potato salad bowl, spooned a final bite into his mouth, and found it tasted exactly like potato salad, which proved nothing and felt like a small betrayal. "This is the hard part," he said. "It still tastes fine. The rule doesn't care how it tastes."

"Most rules don't," said Mr. Krause.

Christian carried the bowl to the trash and stood over it for one more second, then tipped the whole thing in, mayonnaise and potatoes and the last of the afternoon, and set the empty bowl in the sink with a clatter that felt decisive and a little sad. "Eggs go back in the fridge," he announced. "Coleslaw's a survivor. Somebody write down when we got home."

"I'll get the marker," said Mr. Krause, and went for the junk drawer.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: A 2013 study led by John Cook examined 11,944 climate paper abstracts and found that 97.1 percent of those taking a position endorsed human-caused global warming.
story:
Coralie set her fork down before she'd cut anything, which her mother would have called a tell. Across the table, her father was saying it again, the thing he'd said at Thanksgiving and again at the funeral in March: that the scientists themselves couldn't agree, that half of them said the climate was warming because of people and half said it wasn't, and that anyone who claimed otherwise was trying to shut down the argument.

"Do they, though," she said. Not a question, the way she'd practiced it in the car, because Rory had told her that if she sounded like she was asking permission, her father would take the whole floor.

"Of course they do. It's a real debate, Coralie. It's not settled."

Rory had come over on Sunday with printouts, because Rory still printed things, spreading them across Coralie's bed like evidence at a trial. The study had a lead author named John Cook, from 2013, and Rory had highlighted the numbers in yellow: eleven thousand nine hundred and forty-four abstracts of climate papers, and among the ones that took a position at all, 97.1 percent endorsed human-caused global warming. Not fifty. Not close to fifty. Coralie had read the pages twice, and then a third time that night with her door shut, tracing the method with her finger, the way the papers had been sorted and rated, and how the ratings were checked by multiple people against each other. "It's not one guy's opinion," Rory had said. "It's a stack of studies, and other researchers went back over the stack. That's the whole point. It got replicated." Coralie had liked that word, replicated, the sense of something being done again on purpose, in daylight.

"There was a study," she said now. "In 2013. John Cook led it. They looked at the abstracts of almost twelve thousand climate papers. Eleven thousand nine hundred and forty-four." Her father's eyebrows went up at the precision, which she had hoped for. "And of the abstracts that took a position, 97.1 percent endorsed human-caused global warming."

Her mother reached for the water pitcher and didn't pour. Her father said, "One study. You're quoting me one study."

"That's the thing," Coralie said, and she could feel the argument tipping, the way a seesaw tips when the kid on the other end shifts their weight. "It's not one study, it's almost twelve thousand of them. And the Cook paper itself got reviewed before it was published, and other people checked the ratings afterward. It's not one result, Dad. It's a field checking its own work for years and getting the same answer."

He was quiet for a moment, and she watched him arrive at his fallback, the one she'd anticipated at one in the morning with the printouts on her chest. "Even so," he said. "Science has been wrong before. Consensus isn't proof. Everyone agreed about all kinds of things that turned out to be wrong."

This was harder, because he was partly right, and Coralie had known he was partly right, lying awake. Consensus wasn't proof. But it also wasn't nothing, and the difference between nothing and not-proof seemed like the actual work of thinking, the part nobody put on a poster. "Fine," she said. "It's not proof. But when 97 out of 100 of the people who took a position land on the same side, and they keep landing there when the studies are redone, that's not a coin flip either. That's evidence about the evidence. And pretending it's fifty-fifty, that's not skepticism, that's just innumeracy with better manners."

Her mother laughed, once, into her napkin, and her father looked at his plate. Coralie waited for the counterattack, the pivot to jobs or electricity bills or her uncle in Alberta.

Instead he said, "Where did you get all that?"

"Rory. And I read the paper myself. We're doing debate prep. Ms. Njoroge has us arguing the carbon tax next week, and I drew the side against it, which is why I know the other stuff too. The deleterious effects on households, all of it." She hated the side she'd drawn, and had told Ms. Njoroge so, and Ms. Njoroge had said that a polity that can't hear its own strongest opposing arguments gets worse at governing, not better, and had refused to switch her. Coralie was still not sure that was fair. It might have been excellent teaching. It might also have been Ms. Njoroge deciding that Coralie in particular needed the discipline, and there was something unbearable about being legible like that.

Her father cut his chicken, finally. "Fifty-fifty was something I heard somewhere," he said. "I don't remember where." He said it quietly, like he was reporting a fact about a stranger. "Your uncle, probably. He likes to proselytize."

"You don't have to concede," Coralie said, too fast, and heard how much she wanted him to, and how that wanting had nothing to do with the abstracts, eleven thousand nine hundred and forty-four of them, 97.1 percent, numbers she would defend anywhere but numbers that weren't, actually, the point of this table.

"I'm not conceding anything," her father said. "Ask your mother to pass the potatoes. And bring the printouts Thursday, I want to see this Cook thing myself."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Many driving courses teach keeping at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead, and a longer gap in rain, snow or darkness.
story:
Samantha had until Friday to learn what three years of being driven around had never taught her: how a car behaves when it is hers. The test was scheduled for nine in the morning at the depot on Fell Street, and the parallel parking alone had already cost her a traffic cone, lent by Mr. Hamdan from the row he used to mark off the staff lot. He taught chemistry and lived two doors down, and he had watched her stall the borrowed sedan twice before offering the cone and the empty school lot on Sunday afternoons.

"Line up your rear axle with their bumper," he said, standing well back with his hands in his pockets. "Then turn the wheel all the way and creep backwards until you're at forty-five degrees. It's geometry, not courage." He refused to say more than that. He believed, or claimed to believe, that anything explained twice was never learned once, and Samantha suspected he extended this philosophy to his chemistry classes out of laziness, though the cone was real enough.

Her friend Maxim sat in the passenger seat for the highway part, because her mother would not do it and Mr. Hamdan had drawn the line at merging. Maxim was an aesthete about cars in a way Samantha was not; he could identify a model by the sound of its door closing, and he kept a folder of photographs of dashboard lighting taken at dusk. He was also calm in the way of people who have decided nothing is their fault. "The on-ramp is a rumor until you're on it," he said. "Match their speed and pick your hole." She merged four times that Tuesday evening, white-knuckled, and each time the hole appeared and the highway accepted her, and she began to internalize the fact that the other drivers were not hunting her, only enduring her.

The following distance was the thing she could not feel. Maxim had told her once, offhand, that you keep at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead, and a longer gap in rain, snow or darkness. He said it the way he said everything, as a matter of taste, like which headlight design he preferred. She had nodded. Now, alone in the school lot before the last practice on Wednesday, she tried to make the numbers mean something. She followed her mother's car down Fell Street at dusk, watching for a sign, any sign, and when the car ahead passed the billboard for the credit union she counted under her breath, one thousand one, one thousand two, and only then did she reach the billboard herself. Two seconds. It felt enormous. Every instinct in her said the space was an invitation to be cut off, and every cut she suffered, the sedan sliding in ahead of her with its blinker still ticking, she reclaimed the gap again, counting, easing off the gas.

I started keeping the tally in my head like a penance. Thursday it rained, a thin cold rain that made the road the color of slate, and I doubled the count out loud, one thousand one through one thousand six, because the rule Maxim had recited was not a suggestion for weather like this. A man in a gray truck rode my bumper for six blocks, close enough that I could see he was chewing, and I held the count anyway, my hands aching on the wheel from holding still. That night Addisyn texted me a photograph of the study guide she'd made for the written portion, and underneath it: "get some sleep, being exhausted is deleterious to your driving and your personality." I wrote back that I was fine. I was not fine. I had parallel parked the cone lot perfectly nine times and then failed twice in a row for no reason I could name, and the test was in eleven hours.

Addisyn arrived at my door at seven with two coffees and her own car keys. "You're doing the whole route once," she said, "and I'm riding along, and if you talk about the cone I'm getting out." She was the sort of friend who did you favors that were slightly inconvenient for her and never mentioned them again. We did the route. We did the credit union billboard, and this time she counted with me, and when I stretched the count past four in the gray morning light she nodded like a judge at a fair. At the lot I parked between her car and the curb on the first try, straightened, and sat there with the engine running while she checked the distance from the curb with her shoe.

I want to say I walked into the depot on Friday certain, but the truth is I carried both things at once: the geometry Mr. Hamdan had drawn in the air with one finger, and the counting Maxim had tossed off like a preference. One said the world was rules you could execute; the other said it was distances you had to keep feeling for, longer in rain, longer in the dark, because the conditions changed and the number changed with them. I still did not know which idea would hold when an examiner with a clipboard sat beside me and a stranger's car cut in front of me on Fell Street. Both, probably. Neither alone.

The examiner was a small woman with reading glasses on a chain. She slid into the passenger seat, clicked her seatbelt, and said, "Back out and proceed to the street." I checked the mirror, put the car in reverse, and began counting under my breath before I'd gone ten feet.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: François Furet's 1978 book, translated as Interpreting the French Revolution, argued the French should stop treating the Revolution as the key to all of modern French history.
story:
The exhibit hall smelled of dust and lemon polish, and under that, faintly, of the river, whose windows had been open since the building was a customs house two hundred years ago. Justine stood in front of a case of engraved portraits, Robespierre and Danton side by side, each man's face sharpened by the engraver into certainty. Her assignment sheet, folded into quarters in her pocket, asked for a historiographical essay, and Mr. Chen had underlined the word twice: not what happened in 1789, but what historians have said about it since 1800, and why they changed their minds.

She had come here with Amin and Maira because the site was running a day for senior history students, and because none of them could face the library on a Saturday. Maira was copying a caption about the Terror into her phone. Amin was reading the wall panel aloud in a mock-documentary voice, which got them shushed by a guide in a green blazer. Justine wrote nothing. Her notes so far were a list of names, Carlyle, Soboul, Cobban, Furet, arranged in an order she did not yet believe in.

"You look like the paintings," Amin said, nodding at the portraits. "Grim and disaffected."

"I'm thinking."

"Same thing, in your case."

What she was actually doing was remembering her grandmother's kitchen in March, the flashback arriving whole, the way flashbacks do, without permission. She had been explaining her coursework over tea, and her grandmother, who had left school at fifteen and read more than anyone Justine knew, had asked the question that unlocked the whole thing: why did historians stop agreeing about 1789? So Justine had told her. "There's this book," she had said, turning her mug so the handle faced the window, "François Furet's 1978 book, translated as Interpreting the French Revolution. He argued the French should stop treating the Revolution as the key to all of modern French history." Her grandmother had repeated the title slowly, getting the French sounds wrong, and Justine had tried to correct the phonetics of it, "Furet, like fur plus é," until they were both laughing, and her grandmother had said, "So they loved it too much to see it," and Justine had written that down on the back of a shopping receipt, because it seemed truer than anything in her textbook.

Amin appeared at her shoulder now, breaking the memory. "Maira's found the letters," he said. "Real ones. Some family that fled to this coast."

The letters lay in a shallow drawer under glass, faded brown ink on paper gone soft as cloth. The site had transcribed one of them onto a card, and Justine read it standing up, one hand pressed flat on the top of the case, cool through her palm.

You ask whether we were right to leave. I do not know how to answer. Here the river smells different and the bread is different and my sister will not speak of Paris at all. She says the past is a country we have been expelled from. I say only that I miss it, and that missing a thing is not the same as judging it.

Maira read it over her shoulder and exhaled. "That's basically your essay."

"It's the opposite of my essay. He can't decide. I'm supposed to decide."

"Are you, though?"

Justine looked at the engraving again, at Robespierre's face rendered so that doubt seemed structurally impossible, and she felt the day sensitizing her to something she could not yet phrase: that the argument between historians was not about facts but about what a country is allowed to need its past to be. The Marxist historians had needed the Revolution as an engine of history, a hinge on which everything after turned. Furet had said, in effect, put the key down. And the man who wrote this letter had put his key down, or had it taken, and could not tell whether he was free or bereft.

She took out her notes and, leaning on the case, drew a line under her list of names and wrote beneath it: two ways of loving the same events. Then she crossed out "loving" and wrote "needing" and let both words stay visible, the crossing out part of the thought. On the bus home she would sit with Maira and Amin and argue it out, and on Sunday she would call her grandmother and read her the letter, and she would still not know whether her own essay should end with the historians or with the man by the different river. She folded the paper along its worn creases. Outside the window, the light on the water shifted as a cloud moved, and she watched it go.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something that a character on stage does not, which lets a short scene build tension quickly.
story:
Addison spread the pages across her grandmother's kitchen table, which still smelled faintly of the coffee her grandfather used to lionize, holding forth every morning about the superiority of beans ground by hand. He had been dead two years now, but the house kept his opinions, and the summer drama program kept its deadline: a ten-minute play, drawn from her own life, staged in the church hall by Friday.

The moment she had chosen was the night her mother found the envelope from the conservatory admissions office and put it, unopened, in the drawer beneath the dish towels. Addison had been sixteen. She had known what was in it because she had checked the portal on her phone, and she had said nothing while her mother fried plantains and talked about the neighbor's car troubles, and the envelope sat in the drawer like a held breath.

She had the scene written but it lay flat on the page. Two people washing dishes, talking about nothing. She read it aloud to the empty kitchen, to the sardonic portrait of her grandfather that hung above the stove, its raised eyebrow seeming to ask whether she intended to bore him posthumously. Then she set the pages down and went to find her grandmother, who was shelling peas on the porch.

"Could I move the desk lamp in the back room?" Addison asked. "For the play." Her grandmother looked up, thumbs paused in the pod. "Which part is the play?" Addison hesitated, because the honest answer was the envelope, and the envelope involved her mother, who was her grandmother's daughter. "The night before I told Mom about the acceptance," she said finally. Her grandmother was quiet long enough for a pea to drop into the bowl. "Take the lamp," she said. "And take the good extension cord, not the one that shocks you."

Fatoumata came over the next afternoon with a bag of tangerines and the reluctance of a gourmand offered snacks she considered beneath her, though she ate three. Mr. Rahman, the retired teacher from next door, had offered his opinions on structure through the fence that morning, and Addison had thanked him and gone inside. She wanted to solve it herself, or mostly herself.

"Read the stage directions," Addison told Fatoumata, arranging the desk lamp so its circle of light fell on the small table she had carried in from the porch. In the revised script, the mother entered first, alone, and took the envelope from her pocket. She did not open it. She placed it in the drawer, under the dish towel, and left. Only then did the daughter enter with the groceries, calling out about the neighbor's car, and the scene that had seemed inert now tightened with every line.

"It's like we're waiting for a bomb," Fatoumata said, chin on her fist, the third tangerine forgotten. "Because we saw her hide it." Addison felt the click of it, the principle assembling itself out of what she had done almost by instinct. "Mr. Rahman called it dramatic irony," she said. "The audience knows something the character on stage doesn't." Fatoumata pointed at her. "Say that part again in the talkback, people will think you're smart."

Addison did not sleep well that night, and not only from nerves. The device worked, she was certain it worked, the audience would lean forward. But she kept imagining her mother in the third row, watching herself hide the letter, and Addison could not decide whether that was a betrayal or a gift. Her mother had been afraid, that was the truth under the scene; afraid the acceptance meant her daughter would leave, afraid of saying so. Staging the hiding made the audience feel the fear. It also made her mother feel it, in public, from people who would never otherwise know. She sat on the floor of the back room with the lamp still on and held both truths at once, unable to rank them.

On Friday she taped the letter to the inside of the drawer herself, angled so the first row could read the conservatory's crest. Her grandmother came early and sat in the front with her good handbag. When the lights came up on the mother alone with the envelope, Addison stood in the wings, script rolled in her fist, watching the audience go still. Somewhere out there was her mother, arriving late, taking the seat at the end of the third row. The mother on stage opened the drawer.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A preprint is a paper posted publicly before peer review, so its findings have not yet been checked by independent experts chosen by a journal.
story:
The public library had one table by the window that got the good light after four o'clock, and Angelina had claimed it with her bag, her jacket, and an iced coffee she was not technically supposed to have. Spread in front of her were two articles, both about whether later school start times improved adolescent sleep, and a blank document on her laptop with the cursor blinking in a paragraph that had no sentences yet.

Mr. Schneider, the reference librarian, drifted past with a cart of returns. "Critical review?" he asked, glancing at her screen.

"Comparative," she said. "Two articles, same question, and I have to say which one argues it better. Or whether they're both wrong. It's due Friday."

"Ah," he said, and kept pushing the cart, which was the correct amount of help.

The first article, the sleep lab study, had come out of a journal with a long name and a cover date and an editorial board listed in tiny print on the inside cover. The second one, the statewide district analysis, had data she liked better, bigger numbers, longer follow-up, but she had found it on a server she'd never heard of, and at the top of the first page, above the title, sat a banner she had been ignoring for two days. She typed the first sentence of her review, deleted it, and typed it again, this time with the word "however" in it, which she also deleted.

Melody dropped into the other chair at half past four, unwrapping a sandwich she'd smuggled past the front desk with more confidence than Angelina had managed with the coffee. "How's the paper of doom?"

"Fine," Angelina said. "Except one of my articles is broken."

"Broken how?"

Angelina turned the laptop so the banner faced Melody. It said, in cheerful institutional blue, PREPRINT. "It was never in a journal. I found the same title in a database and there's nothing there. It's just on this server, sitting there."

Melody chewed for a moment. "My brother does this. A preprint is a paper posted publicly before peer review, so its findings haven't been checked by independent experts chosen by a journal."

"Your brother's a scientist now?"

"He's a first year. He says it a lot." Melody took another bite. "So don't use it?"

"That's not the assignment, though." Angelina pulled the laptop back and minimized the banner as if it were something she could shut in a drawer. "The assignment is to weigh them. And the preprint has the better data. Five thousand students, two full years, the journal one has ninety kids for eight weeks." She heard herself building a defense and distrusted it, the way you distrust any argument that arrives exactly when you need it.

Randy arrived at five with a printed schedule he wanted Melody to approve, some seismic shift in his fall courses that he described as though it were a hostage negotiation, and he stood at the end of the table offering commentary on everything, including the sandwich, until Melody told him to sit down or leave. He sat down. Within four minutes he had picked up the sleep lab article and begun reading the abstract out loud in a documentary voice, which got him nothing.

Angelina let them argue about whether the college's new writing requirement was a plot and did her own thinking underneath it. The detractors of the preprint, as far as she could tell from a search that took her through three comment threads and one blog with a grudge, weren't saying the data was fake. They were saying nobody had checked it, which was a different objection, and harder to write around, because "it might be fine" is not a sentence you can put in an academic review and survive. She tried suturing the two papers together, a paragraph where the small lab study and the huge district analysis confirmed each other, and it worked beautifully, which made her suspicious. When two things agree that neatly, she thought, either you've found something true or you've found something convenient, and the review was supposed to be about knowing the difference.

She deleted the beautiful paragraph. Then she wrote a plainer one: the journal study was small but vetted; the preprint was large but unvetted; both pointed the same direction; she could not fully certify the second. Then she sat looking at the sentence "I cannot fully certify the second" and thought it made her sound like a notary.

At quarter to six Mr. Schneider came back through with his empty cart. "Dead cursor or dead document?"

"Dead confidence," Angelina said.

"That's usually Tuesday," he said. "You're ahead of schedule."

Melody leaned over her shoulder and read the screen. "Just say the preprint hasn't been peer reviewed yet and that's a limitation. That's honest."

"It's more than a limitation," Angelina said. "It's the whole reason the paper's different. If I tuck it into a limitations paragraph I'm pretending I weighed it the same as the other one, and I didn't." Randy, who had been quietly folding his schedule into smaller and smaller squares, said, "So lead with it. Say why you're still using it anyway." She looked at him. He shrugged. "It's your paper. I just work here."

She sat with her hands off the keyboard for a minute, watching the light move across the table toward the iced coffee, which had gone watery and illegal. Then she opened a new paragraph and typed the sentence she'd been circling for two days: the question wasn't which article to trust, it was how much trust each one had earned, and by what process, and she was going to put the process in the first paragraph instead of the last one. Her conclusion, she decided, could end where the evidence ended, short of certainty, and if the professor wanted a tidy verdict she could want one back.

At six the overhead lights came on automatically, harsh against the window's last blue. Melody gathered her sandwich wrapper, Randy pocketed his folded square, and Angelina copied the citation for the preprint, banner and all, into her references page. "Eight o'clock tomorrow," she said to no one in particular, packing her bag. "Same table."
